utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, once again. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone. Laurie Sartorio and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution, assisted by Alma Imamovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson appearing today on behalf of General Rasim Delic, together with our assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And how do you feel today, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you took and you made at the beginning of your testimony, to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujezinovic. We're going to return back to the Rules of Services for the Military Police of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a document we looked at yesterday. Your Honours, if we could please look at Exhibit 586.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the exhibit, can you confirm, Mr. Mujezinovic, that this document was in force throughout the war, once it was introduced in used in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was in force the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see here that the first chapter of the rules deals with the sphere of activity and the tasks of the military police. Would you agree with me that if we look at paragraph number 1, we can see that the tasks of the military police included uncovering and preventing criminal activities involving members of the armed forces, and also it involved dealing with criminal offences within the jurisdiction of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at the next page in the B/C/S version, but keep the same page here in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph number 2, could you confirm that what this paragraph talks about is that in matters of investigation in the pre-trial stage of proceedings, the military police are to be fully autonomous where members of the armed forces are suspected of being perpetrators of criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the rules read, and that's how things were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is turn to the chapter on command and control that you touched upon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This can be found at page 5 of the English version and page 6 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, may I just interrupt you for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I forgot at the beginning to mention that we still continue pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the same reason as yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So from paragraph 7, which you discussed yesterday ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can perhaps turn over into the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: ... in terms of command and control, we can see that the military police is commanded and controlled by the senior officer; in other words, the commander of the unit to which the military police was attached. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is commanded by the commander of the unit, the part of which the relevant military police unit is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the commander of the unit was responsible, therefore, for issuing certain orders to the military police, such as the use of the military police in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It was only the commander of that unit who could use the unit of the military police, in the full sense of the word, during combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So in respect of your particular military police unit, the 3rd Military Police Battalion, in that case it was the 3rd Corps commander that was responsible for issuing such orders?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, only the 3rd Corps command -- commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And although it was the decision of the commander of the unit whether or not to use the military police in combat activities, the assistant commander for security was able to propose to the commander of the unit the use of the military police in combat activities; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. These are his authorities -- or rather, the scope of his authority and what he can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now what I'd like to do is turn our attention to paragraph number 8, which you told us yesterday provides that, in professional terms, the military police was headed by the senior officer of the Military Security Service of the unit to which the military police was attached. Just so we're clear about it, this senior officer of the Military Security Service normally went by the title of "Assistant Commander for Security"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In different intervals, he was called "Assistant Commander for Security" in the corps, or "Chief of Security" within command of the 3rd Corps; however, it was the same scope of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So in addition to the military police being under the command and control of the commander of the unit, there was a professional line for reporting and ordering of certain tasks, and what I'd like to ask you about is the sorts of tasks that the assistant commander for security could order to the military police. Is it right that the assistant commander for security could order the Military Police Battalion -- unit, I should say, to, for example, go to a crime scene or to carry out investigation of certain matters?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could. He had the authority to send a part of the military police unit to the scene to carry out an on-site investigation and other matters belonging to the pre-trial stage of proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the assistant commander for security would not need the approval of the commander of the unit in order to direct the military police unit to go and carry out these sorts of tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commander of the military police unit [as interpreted] was a subordinate professional organ; therefore, he needn't necessarily ask for his consent when issuing such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. The witness said "the commander of the military police unit." Should it be "the commander of the Military Security Service unit"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: That's what I heard, Your Honour, in my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Witness, could you just clarify a point? Did you say that the commander of the Military Security Service was a subordinate professional organ and, therefore, he didn't necessarily ask for consent from the commander of the unit when issuing such an order?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is somewhat confusing. Perhaps it has to do with the matter of languages. In any case, he was never commander of the Military Security. What you had was Assistant Commander of the Corps for Security, or Chief of the Security Service within the Command of the 3rd Corps. Those were the full titles of the organ or the person that was professionally in charge or superior to the commander of the military police unit of the 3rd Corps. That person could order the use of a part of the MP Battalion in exercising certain investigative tasks, without prior consultation or approval on my part, since I was commander of the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, that's throwing a little spanner in the works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, he wouldn't need your approval to direct certain investigative tasks; but, similarly, he wouldn't need the approval of the commander of the unit in order to direct the military police to carry out certain investigative tasks as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that for serious criminal matters, rather than instructing the military police to carry out activities, the assistant commander for security could direct members of the Military Security Service to gather information and to deal with the matter?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In implementing investigative tasks, the chief of military security had the authority to make use of some people from within his own service or people from the military police, according to what he saw fit to implement those tasks. He did not necessarily need to turn to members of the military police alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd just like to turn our attention to military police units at the level subordinate to the corps level. It's right to say that there were military police units within each division and within each brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that the number of military police officers within a brigade would depend upon the size of the brigade. So, in some instances, there could be a company of military police or there could be a platoon. In respect of the 328th Brigade, do you know what sort of military police unit was attached to that unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was a military police platoon, since it was a mountain brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what you told us, a moment ago, about the principles of command and control and reporting, that also applies at the brigade level as well; and by that, what I mean is that the brigade commander exercised command and control over the brigade military police unit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The Rules of Service defined the relationship. The principal is absolutely the same. Commander of the MP platoon is subordinate to the brigade commander within which that military police unit is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in professional terms, the military police unit would report to the assistant commander for security within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, it follows that the commander of a brigade could order a military police unit within his brigade unit to carry out activities which required the use of force in order to make sure that criminal acts were stopped and the perpetrators were found and discovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the reporting that you made to both the commander of your unit and the assistant commander for security, in the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution, you said that you would report to the commander on operational issues. How often would you report to him?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. As far as regular activities went, without significant combat operations, in principle, we would have briefings twice monthly with the corps commander. When there was immediate combat activity, the briefing to the corps commander was done according to the situation. Most frequently, it was once a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right that you would also report to the assistant commander for security. Would you report to him on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of security, we would forward written reports, daily, weekly, and monthly reports. And upon his request, in principle, at least once a month, there was oral briefing or reporting on the activities of the MP Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to a rather different issue, and that is the obligation of the military police to file criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, if we can look at the document that's on the screen in front of us, what I'm interested in is paragraph number 6, which it may be on this page in the English, and I believe it's on page 3 in the B/C/S version. Perhaps we can just scroll to the top. I think what we're going to have to do is go to page 3 in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can see that paragraph number 6 is within a new chapter, chapter number 2, which is headed "Tasks of the Military Police," and what paragraph 6 says is: "In line with the sphere of their activity, the military police shall carry out the following tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the task at part F, which is at page 4 in the English version, and it's at page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, in talking about the military police, "F" deals with prevention and further detection of criminal activity, and what it says is: "In line with their legally authorised power, they conduct investigation work in pre-trial proceedings when the perpetrators of the crimes are members of the armed forces or other civilians but only in cases where the object of the crime is military property or if these are crimes within the competence of the military courts." Mr. Mujezinovic, are you familiar with this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that what this does is it provides an obligation on the part of the military police to investigate criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The military police had the authority and obligation to undertake these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in respect of that, I'd now like to consider the powers of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we could please turn to page 6 of the English document and page 8 of the B/C/S version, and it's paragraph 11 that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can see here a heading "Chapter 4, Powers and Services of the Military Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that there's a -- that the number 11 is missing out. If you look slightly above the heading, you can see that chapter 10 precedes this. If we look at the B/C/S version, it should follow that chapter 11 comes after the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is that so, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence -- in terms of sequence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So paragraph 11 provides that: "In carrying out the duties of their service, members of the military police implement the following measures and actions." Here, we can see a list of the powers of the military police, and it's right, isn't it, that the third entry here refers to filing reports?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Powers of the military police were organised in a way to secure the legality when we conducted our activities. Filing reports would understand filing both disciplinary and criminal reports in such cases when the relevant military police units established that the circumstances under which a criminal offence was committed is of that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exactly. And if we can now look at paragraph 15, which carries on from what you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is at page 7 in the English and page 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see here that this paragraph states: "The military police file reports: When a person refuses to comply with a caution, refuses to be identified, commits an infringement of military discipline or a serious disturbance of the peace, endangers the safety of traffic on the roads, commits a crime which is prosecuted ex officio, and also when detaining and bringing into custody." Now, my question is: Would you agree, from what we've just seen and from these rules, that there was an obligation on all military policemen to gather information about crimes that had occurred that either involved members of the armed forces or fell within the jurisdiction of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, it is the same, whether they were committed by members of the army or whether they are under the competence of the military courts. Only under those circumstances, members of the military police have the power and duty to collect security-related information in order to have a full scope of investigative and pre-investigative tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We've talked about the duty on the military police to file a criminal report. Yesterday, in your testimony, you said that the military police was required to prepare a criminal report and follow it -- forward it to the relevant court. Would you agree with me that, in fact, the military police was obliged to send the criminal report to the competent district military prosecutor and not to the military court?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. The competent prosecutor assesses the validity and the basis of the criminal report, and forwards it up the chain perhaps by opening a file, a case against the perpetrators for which the file or report had been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in terms of sending a criminal report to the competent district military prosecutor, is it correct that the authorised officers of the military police were required to do this independently, without any further approval from their professional or superior command?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional superior organ needn't necessarily be consulted on these activities. In yesterday's presentation, I tried to clarify the procedure relating to communicating -- to the communication between an official, an authorised official, and an investigative judge. The investigative military judge had the authority to direct the investigation in keeping with the law and perhaps to provide specific instruction to the authorised official of the military police, so that a potential crime could be fully documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The question that I put, and just to clarify it, a military police officer didn't need approval before he filed a criminal report with the district military prosecutor, did he? If he saw that a crime had been committed, he could do that immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't need an approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get clarification? Would he not need, in any case, to report to - I must make sure I get the correct title - to report to the chief of the security service within the command of the 3rd Corps? I'm not saying "seek approval," but to report, just to report that such-and-such a thing has happened, and "I've sent a report to the prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When a report is submitted, the chief of the Military Security Service had to be informed. That was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could turn to document D704, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, can you confirm that what we have in front of us is a document headed: "Report for August 1993", dated the 3rd of September, 1993, from the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion to the 3rd Corps chief of security? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By format, it's a document implying the drafting of a report about the activity of the Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could please look at the last page in both documents, just to see who the author was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that the document bears your name. Is that your signature, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my name and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to the first page in both documents, please. If we can go to the bottom of the page in English, and that's good in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see here a heading. It says: "Number 3. Application of military police measures against members of the BH Army." Would you agree with me that within this section, what you're doing is providing information to the 3rd Corps chief of security about the actions carried out by the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You're explaining the numbers of army members that have had their identity checked, you're informing him about the numbers of people that have been brought into detention, and also you're talking about check-points and the stopping of military and civilian vehicles. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can just go to the next page in the B/C/S, and to the top there.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This is a form of reporting of the MP Battalion of the 3rd Corps to the chief of security of the 3rd Corps, where, more or less, it's done by services and by authorities. This is a report about -- to the chief about measures and activities undertaken by the battalion in the month. That is the subject of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could turn our attention to the next section, which is headed: "Number 4. Criminal and disciplinary reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree that we can read in this section that 24 criminal reports were submitted by the Military Police Battalion to the District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You can see from the report that these are 24 criminal charges against a total of 32 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the next paragraph down, we can see that included within those criminal reports, there were two reports for war crimes against the civilian population; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that from the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So from this report, we can conclude that in August 1993, the Military Police Battalion were filing criminal reports against members of the ARBiH, and also that they did file criminal reports for war crimes as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, both criminal reports against persons and for which action are -- the responsibility lies with the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can put this document away, and I'd like to show a similar document, which is E871. Your Honours, before I do that, please, could I tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document D704 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit 877.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: E871. While we're waiting for the document to come up, I can just explain that this is a report on criminal reports and requests for disciplinary procedure filed in the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Mr. Mujezinovic, that this report is dated the 28th of July, 1995, and it went from the 3rd Military Police Battalion to the 3rd Corps Military Security Service?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In form, it's a document or a report made by the 3rd Corps MP Battalion with [as interpreted] the chief of the security of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to the last page in both documents again, just to see who the author is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant by "with the chief of the security of the 3rd Corps"? You're dealing with the form of the document, and I don't understand how part of the form of the document includes the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, can you clarify that? The question I'd asked you was: "Could you confirm that it went to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to the first page while we clarify this issue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you answer the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document or a report that the MP Battalion sent to the chief of security of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That makes better sense. What do you call this part of speech? The word "with" didn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we could please go to the last pages in both documents again, just to ascertain the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version, we can see that it bears your name, Mr. Mujezinovic. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my name and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Returning back to the first page, please, it's the first paragraph of the document that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that it states: "In the period between 1st of July, 1995 and 30th of July, 1995, the Services Department of the 3rd Military Police Battalion filed, before the competent prosecutor's offices in Zenica, 27 criminal reports against 31 persons ..." And then, in the second paragraph, it states: "During the same period, the Services Department of the 3rd Military Police Battalion filed 21 requests for disciplinary action against 24 persons." So, once again, this document shows that during July 1995, the Military Police Battalion was filing criminal reports with the competent District Military Prosecutor's Office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. In accordance with the authority of the military police, you can see that both criminal and disciplinary charges were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we've seen two of these sorts of documents. Were these sorts of reports being sent every month, setting out the numbers of criminal reports that had been filed?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The MP Battalion was obliged to draft a monthly report about submitted or filed criminal charges, or initiated requests for the establishment of disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: The document we looked at for August 1993 talked about 24 criminal reports against 32 people, and this document for July 1995 talks about 27 criminal reports against 31 people. Are these sorts of numbers of criminal reports being issued each month typical?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to talk about an average number of filed charges. Depending on the general situation, the number of criminal acts would increase. So, in principle, it was 30 to 40 such charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thirty to forty such charges per month; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. Because like I say, it's very hard to say that, in view of the circumstances in which all of that was happening, especially in situations that were conditioned by the general environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And before we move away from the issue of sending criminal reports, in respect of military police at the brigade level, would you agree with me that it would be wrong for somebody to suggest that the only duty of the military police at that level was to simply collect information and to send it to their professional superior, the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was definitely not their only duty. Units at that level of military police had the same duties and authorities as military police units of a higher rank. So, that MP unit also physically had to provide security for the brigade command. They had to patrol in certain areas. And, of course, along with all of that, they had to gather data on specific criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You say it wasn't -- it definitely was not their only duty. They had the obligation to file criminal reports, didn't they, if they discovered that a crime had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, staying at the brigade level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask: Did they also have the duty to submit criminal reports to the military prosecutor where crimes had been committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're nodding your head. For the sake of the record, could you please say in words what you mean by nodding the head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The military police unit was obliged to pass on the report to the authorised prosecutor's office; and at the same time, provided a copy of the report to the assistant security commander of the brigade in which he was active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in relation to the military police at the brigade level, if a situation occurred where a military police officer found out that a crime had taken place, and he sends a report to his superior only, the assistant commander for security, would you agree with me that his duty to investigate did not cease; he still had the duty to continue to gather evidence and then submit a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. His duty was still to continue to collect evidence and complete the report; and, of course, the security organs needed to be expertly directed and instructed, if the situation required it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to turn our attention to the Military Security Service. Now, if I could refer you to another document, which is the Rules of Operation for the Military Security Service in the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's Exhibit 585. Perhaps if we can go to the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, here, we can see the cover. Were you familiar with these rules, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the expert sense, I'm not familiar with this rule, because it deals with the procedure of the Military Security Service and not that of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. We can see that it is dated September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can -- Your Honours, this document is a little bit different from my version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you work with the version that is before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. If we can go to the first page of both documents. I apologise. Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that, from the top of the document, that these rules were issued by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is. As I said, I was not in the position to use this rule or to apply it in everyday activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can refer to paragraph 27, please, which is at page number 7 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 27, we can see that: "Authorised officers of the Military Security Service have the right and duty to undertake prescribed measures and actions vis-a-vis individuals, groups, and organisations," et cetera. You see that, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in this connection, if we could now look at paragraph 31, which is at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, and it's on the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could just take a look at that paragraph, do you agree that this paragraph provides that, in order to carry out the tasks in his field, an authorised officer of the Military Security Service is entitled to check the identity of members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that's what it says in the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Then if we can go into paragraph 32 in the B/C/S, it's the same page in the English. It's the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Here, it provides that: "In matters concerning criminal offences within the jurisdiction of military courts and which are prosecuted ex officio, authorised officers of the Military Security Service may arrest a suspect and bring him immediately before an investigating judge of the military court or the nearest military command or unit." You see that, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, finally, in this connection, paragraph 33 provides that: "An authorised officer of the Military Security Service and military police may arrest military personnel or workers serving in the armed forces if caught in the commission of a criminal offence." Would you agree with me that this, these rules, clearly provide that both members of the Military Security Service and the military police have powers to arrest people, if it appears that a criminal offence has occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Remaining with this issue, if we could look at the chapter dealing with the Military Security Service in criminal proceedings, which is at page number 9 in the English. I believe it might be the next page in the B/C/S. It's paragraph 40 that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, here, we can see the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Here, we can read that it says: "When there is reasonable suspicion that a criminal offence triable by military courts has been committed, officers of the Military Security Service must take the necessary measures to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence, to prevent the perpetrator or his accomplice from going into hiding or escaping, to uncover and protect the evidence and exhibits which can serve as evidence, and to gather all the information useful for successful conduct of the criminal proceedings." Now, yesterday, you were asked by the Prosecutor if there was any other organ in the ARBiH that had jurisdiction to investigate crimes. Would you agree that from looking at these rules, it's clear that members of the Military Security Service also had the possibility and obligation to take steps to arrest and investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My response, yesterday, referred to a specially-organised unit, whose main task would be to implement these activities in terms of collection of data. The authorities of the Military Security Service were greater than the authority of the military police, so that the Military Security Service had an absolute duty to compile the necessary data, to document everything, and to submit a criminal report. As part of that, they could use, but did not necessarily have to, members of the military police who were subordinated to it along the professional line. It had to -- it could, but it didn't have to, act in cooperation and coordination with organs of internal affairs. It could, but did not have to, use the other organs within the Military Security Service. The main task was to document and file a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. And in connection with what you've just said, if we can look at paragraph 41, this provides that: "On the basis of the information gathered, officers of the Military Security Service in the command of the brigade, or a corresponding or higher ranking officer in the Military Security Service, shall submit a criminal report to the competent military prosecutor's office." So this confirms what you just said, that members of the Military Security Service also had the obligation to file a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then, finally, before we leave this document, if we can briefly look at paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Here, it states: "When the perpetrator of a criminal offence is unknown..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's on the next page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if you could just take a look at this paragraph, would you agree that from this paragraph, even when a perpetrator is unknown, an officer of the Military Security Service is still required to file a criminal report with the competent military prosecutor in cases against an unknown person?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In cases when you could not establish the perpetrator and the criminal act was committed, the person investigating the act, in this case organs of the security service, would need to submit a report according -- or against an unidentified person, meaning that the perpetrator was not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move away from this issue and now discuss the matter of discipline. I believe you told us yesterday, in your evidence, that it was the duty of the commander of a unit to impose disciplinary measures against members of his unit. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, pronounces disciplinary measures for specific disciplinary violations pursuant to the rules relating to military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it follows that the commander of one unit could not discipline members of a different unit; however, in such circumstances, the commander, who sees that a disciplinary matter has occurred, should notify the commander of the other unit responsible for the soldiers in need of discipline. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He is not authorised to carry out disciplinary measures. This is the authority only the superior commander within the command-and-control system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In such a situation where one commander finds out that matters have occurred where disciplinary steps should be taken, where the people carrying out those matters are not his subordinates, the commander should take steps to notify the commander, the other commander, that his subordinates have been carrying out activities which require disciplinary measures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, there are two ways in which a commander of that unit should act. The first would be on the basis of collegiality, to inform the unit commander in writing that his perpetrators have committed a certain disciplinary violation in order to carry out steps. Secondly, he was duty-bound, in his eventual reports to superiors, to suggest that disciplinary violations were committed in another unit in order that the system of command and control -- or through the system of command and control, certain disciplinary measures could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's P2099. This is a document that we looked at yesterday, I believe. My colleague is telling me that we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, the copy is not so good. So if you have any difficulties, please let me know. Would you agree that what we can see here is a document from the 3rd Corps Military Security Department, and it's dated the 23rd of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document from the security sector of the 3rd Corps. This is a document of the MP Battalion of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see that now. I realise my error.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can look at the second page in both the B/C/S and English versions, so we can ascertain the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We see here that your name appears on the document. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I think it is correct to say that this is a document from you, providing information to the 3rd Corps Military Security Service. If we can look at what it's about, in the first paragraph, it states: "In accordance with the order of the 3rd Corps commander, 03/1-217-943, of the 23rd of May, 1995, commanders of units are held responsible for resolving request for initiating disciplinary action. "After the disciplinary procedure has been finished, the original unit, more precisely the commander of the unit, needs to form the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police of the aforementioned disciplinary measures taken after requests for initiating disciplinary responsibility that were submitted by the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police." We can see, from the second paragraph, that you go on to say that: "The 3rd Battalion of the Military Police has so far sent 20 requests for establishing disciplinary responsibility of members of the 3rd Corps units." Could you just explain to us a little about this document? Is it correct that what's happened here is that you have notified commanders of certain units that they should carry out disciplinary measures in respect of members of their units? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the order of the corps commander and the rule book on military discipline, as well as the Rules of Service for the Military Police in its part pertaining to the authority of the military police, where it is stated that it can submit reports, the MP Battalion submitted requests to initiate disciplinary proceedings to the unit commanders, the members of which had committed a certain disciplinary breach. The commanders of these units, in keeping with the corps commander's order, had a duty to inform back the MP Battalion on the measures they undertook against the people who had criminal -- disciplinary reports submitted against them. It is all contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it appears from this document that certain units had not reported back to you about disciplinary measures taken, and we can see that from paragraph 3, and there you list the units; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The units and perpetrators are specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can turn to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that one of the units to which you had sent a request to issue disciplinary measures and had not reported back to you as to measures taken, at number 5, is the El Mujahedin, or "the El Mujahidir Squad," as it says; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it appears the El Mujahedin Detachment commander had been informed to carry out disciplinary measures in respect of someone called "Emir Imamovic"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was notified by the submitting of the criminal -- of the disciplinary report, and in keeping with the corps commander's instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the person that the El Mujahedin Detachment was supposed to discipline Emir Imamovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can we conclude from this document, dated May 1995, that the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment was not following the order of the 3rd Corps commander to impose disciplinary measures and report back to the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that he did anything wrong, but he did not report back. He may have issued a disciplinary measure, but he never reported back on it, which leads me to conclude that there were no disciplinary measures imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can remember the name, Emir Imamovic, and that this document was sent on the 22nd of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could turn to document P2472 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2742"], please. Your Honours, I tender this document for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P2099 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit 878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: 2472. Your Honours, this does not look like the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the transcript gives two numbers. First it said "2742," and now it says "2472." Which number do you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It should be 2472.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we can see here, Mr. Mujezinovic, that this is a document addressed to the Command of the El Mujahedin Detachment. It's dated the 2nd of August, 1995. It's from the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could just look at the final page, please, to ascertain the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that your name appears on this document. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just find out who signed on the left before we move?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Services Department, Samir Saric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Security Services Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Services Department, which was part of the MP Battalion that I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can revert back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the meaning of this signature on the left of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He authorised the text. It is a subordinate unit, which in the full sense of the word is the true author of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at the first paragraph when it appears, Mr. Mujezinovic. Is it right that this is a document from you to the Command of the El Mujahedin Detachment, in which you refer to the 3rd Corps commander's order of the 3rd of May, 1995, and you request -- and you make him responsible for solving a request for starting a disciplinary procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, in keeping with the Rules of Service of the Military Police and pursuant to the corps commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the person that the request is -- who is the subject of the request, it's Emir Imamovic. So this is the same name that we saw in the last document. Is it so that when you wrote to the El Mujahedin in August 1995, the reason was that -- the reason for that was because they had failed to comply with the request that the commander made in May 1995, some two months prior?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you recall if the El Mujahedin Detachment ever reacted to this document from you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this document could please be admitted into evidence, and I think it's an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, before the break, we were talking about disciplinary measures; and still on this topic, I'd like you to look at Exhibit 867.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was a document we saw yesterday. It's headed: "Status and role of Military Security Service and military police organs in disciplinary matters."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Witness, can you please confirm that this document is dated the 2nd of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could just look at page -- yes, if we can look at this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can we see that it has your name on it towards the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And when you were questioned about this document yesterday, you explained that what we can see is this is a letter with which a document was forwarded to various units. The document bears the title: "Document of the Military Security Administration with instructions for actions of Military Security Service and military police organs in disciplinary matters." Do you remember discussing this document? This was a -- do you recall mentioning this document and explaining what the purpose was of forwarding on to the units the document that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it. The role was to clarify the specific procedures in relation to my unit and the military police, in general, in certain disciplinary cases, and it went for the whole of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the list at the bottom of this page, which shows us who the document was delivered to, would you agree with me that it was not sent to the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see that it was sent to the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if you're able to help us, is there any reason that you're aware of why it wasn't sent to the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document can be put away, and I'm going to turn to the issue of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, you were asked some questions about this detachment yesterday, and you were asked if it had a security organ. Is it correct to say that you were not familiar with the structure of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with the structure of the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And can you help us: Are you able to confirm that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not report to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps or to any other unit of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for the simple reason that I didn't have either information or documents available or on any potential correspondence between the security organ and some other structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If the El Mujahedin Detachment had been a regular ARBiH unit, falling well within the system of command and control, it should have filed a daily report on security matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am truly not familiar with the correspondence or the mutual responsibilities of different security organs within the chain of command and control; therefore, I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you two documents on the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can first of all bring up Exhibit 873, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This is a document that we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, to save some time, I can explain that it is a daily report authored by Mr. Mujezinovic, dated the 29th of August, 1995. If we can just quickly look at the last page in this document. Yes, we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that's your name and signature at the bottom of the page there?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to discuss page number 9 in the English version with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If you just bear with me, it's at -- I believe it's page number 4 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you see there a heading which states: "Engagement of military police unit on day of report"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that in this daily report of the 29th of August, 1995, you are providing information about how the Military Police Battalion has been tasked on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. From the report, one can see what the activities were of the Military Police Battalion on the day of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do, is there any reason why the numbers are cancelled?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you answer that, Mr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask you for a further clarification. Which numbers do you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can see: 7, crossed; 18, crossed; 57 crossed; 87, crossed. All of them, just look at them. If you look at the B/C/S, too, they are crossed and other numbers are written next to the crossed numbers, which actually makes this English version not a true copy of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not focusing on this specific point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, but I'm asking a question. I'm just saying this English version is not a true copy of the B/C/S because there are two numbers in the B/C/S, and whereas there's one in the English version. That's all I'm saying, and I don't think the Court will be inclined to admit this document unless it is corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a document that was tendered by the Prosecution and admitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has it been?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will have to query that. But, anyway, are you able to tender an explanation why the numbers are crossed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that this was a previous report; but in the course of two or three days, the figures were different. However, the categories of engagement were the same. Therefore, I presume that the previous report from the day before was copied and then the old figures were crossed out and some additional numbers written by hand, reflecting the situation on the day of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could bring up the next page in the English version, please. The B/C/S version can remain as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, can you see a heading which states: "Entrance and Exit Control Service checked IDs of the following persons." Do you see that? It's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And below that, we can see a list of names, some of which appear to be the names of military units. Am I right that saying that what we can see here is a list of locations where the Military Police Battalion carried out identity checks during the course of the 29th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem. The heading says "following persons." Now you're saying "locations."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, can you read out the heading, the second heading down that we can see on the B/C/S document? It begins with "Kroz." Can you explain what this section is?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Entrance and Exit Control Service checked the IDs of the following number of persons," and then what follows are the facilities secured by the MP Battalion, as well as four military police units in the divisions and military police platoons within brigades. This is, for example, the security system in item 1, in which the 3rd Corps Command is involved. A number of persons were asked to check -- to have their IDs checked. For example, there's a figure of 80 at Zening facility secured by the MP Battalion. There were no IDs checked; at KP Dom, 17 people; Rudar hotel, 12; and so on and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So all or most of these locations are places at which subordinate units of the 3rd Corps were located; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that on this list ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: ... it shows that no identity checks were carried out at any location held by the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no facility mentioned in this report where the El Mujahedin Detachment was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can just look in the next page in English, just so Their Honours can see the entire section. On this same issue, if we can look at Exhibit 874, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you leave this exhibit, Mr. Wood, why is this English version not identical to the B/C/S document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been informed that we will get a revision of the English, and we can submit that when it's complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. It doesn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: Why is this one, why was it not properly done in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I can't answer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want us to do with this exhibit now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I believe it's already been admitted; and as I indicated, the Prosecution will submit a final translation of this document. I see that it does say "Draft translation." We will submit that as soon as a final translation is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question that I would like to ask to the Prosecution. Yesterday, did we have a look at those pages where all these numbers are, or did we see other pages of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I directed the witness's attention to other pages of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it means that next time, when a whole document is tendered into evidence, we'll have to check the whole document and check whether both versions are identical. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've asked to turn to Exhibit 874. I believe it may be a document that is under seal. I'm not going to be referring to anything that's confidential; but if the Court would wish us to go into private session, then we can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to go into private session? I don't know what questions you're going to ask, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's certainly not going to be anything confidential; but I can see the Registrar is concerned, so, yes, please, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just waiting for the document to appear on the screen. The document is the correct one in English, but I think it's the next page in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, we saw this document yesterday. It's dated the 19th of October, 1995, and it has the heading: "Hand-over of members of the so-called 'VRS' from Detachment El Mujahedin." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just scroll down in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see from this document that one of the persons that signed it was Zakir Alispahic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a document of the 3rd Military Police Battalion, and what it states in the first paragraph is: "On the 29th of September, 1995, based on an agreement with the Security Body of the El Mujahedin Detachment, 3rd Battalion of Military Police took over ten members of the so-called 'VRS.'" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this document speaks of an agreement. If the El Mujahedin Detachment had a security organ that was properly established within the professional line of command in the security chain of the ARBiH, would you agree that there would be no need for any agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a proper command-and-control system, there is an order, not an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Exactly. So if the El Mujahedin Detachment fell properly within the command-and-control system, then a superior command would simply order the El Mujahedin Detachment to hand over these Serb detainees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This document suggests that there was some process of negotiation taking place. Would you agree that this document suggests that the relationship between the El Mujahedin Detachment and the 3rd Military Police Battalion -- or the 3rd Corps, I should say, was one of cooperation, rather than one of a superior/subordinate relationship?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any detachment or military police battalion could not be in a superior/subordinate relationship. But if the Corps Command had issued an order to the El Mujahedin or to the MP Battalion, then it would have to say in this document: "Based on the order of the 3rd Corps, the hand-over was executed," and so on and so forth. So the MP Battalion could not issue orders to any detachment, but the Corps Command could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I would like to understand this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just going to elaborate, and please feel free to expand after I've asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the Military Police Battalion could not have issued any orders to the El Mujahedin Detachment. That's clear. But from this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is not clear to me. That is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, are you able to clarify your earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe, first of all, let me raise the question I wanted to raise with the previous answer first. You're saying, sir, "any detachment or military police battalion could not be in a superior/subordinate relationship." Do I understand that your military police battalion was not in a superior/subordinate relationship within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You do read English? Can you see the answer at line 18 of page 43 what it says? You are recorded as having said, "any detachment or military police battalion could not be in a hand-over was executed," suggesting that your unit was also not in a superior/subordinate relationship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was probably not specific enough. The Military Police Battalion within the B and H Army composition could not order any other formation which was also within the B and H Army to take any steps. It had authority -- it went along the vertical line. The Corps Command that -- that line went from the Corps Command to the Military Police Battalion, and then towards other units of the corps as well. I'm speaking about the situation when I, as the battalion commander of the military police, could not order anyone within the system except my direct subordinate -- subordinates to undertake certain steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But to my question: Do I understand you to say that the Military Police Battalion stood in a superior/subordinate relationship within the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That corrects that problem. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And from this document, we cannot see that any superior unit has ordered the El Mujahedin to hand over the Serb detainees; instead, it talks about the process of agreement. As I understood your evidence earlier, if the El Mujahedin Detachment had been properly within the command-and-control system, you could have expected to see here something saying: Based on the order of the superior unit, the El Mujahedin Detachment was ordered to hand over the Serb detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct. Mr. Alispahic did have the order -- actually, if he did have the order, then at the top of the document Mr. Alispahic would have to note that this was done on the basis of an order and not on the basis of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. While we're on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, but there's still some confusion in my mind. From the answer given from the witness, from the answer that you gave, sir, to Judge Moloto, I understood that the 3rd Battalion of Military Police could not issue orders to the El Mujahedin Detachment, and that the orders should come from the 3rd Corps commander. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Consequently, in the relationship between the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment and the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police, it would have been normal to have an agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Talks and agreements, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your answer, Witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the security organ, while the unit and the Military Police Battalion would talk about and agree on certain activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, how much longer are you still going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just about ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I anticipate about ten or 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're virtually two hours against the Prosecution's one hour 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll be as brief as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mujezinovic, if I can just clarify that. If we can put the El Mujahedin Detachment to one side, and if we talked about another detachment falling below the 3rd Corps, I may be speaking hypothetically here, the other detachment having a security organ, it's right, isn't it, that through the professional line of reporting, the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps could order the security organ of that other detachment to carry out certain actions. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So there wouldn't be any process of talking or agreement between the 3rd Corps Military Security Service and the security organ of that other detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wouldn't. The Military Security Service is a superior organ, and in that case can issue an order both to that unit's security organ or to the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So based on what you've just said, the Military Security Service could issue an order. In this document here that talks about the El Mujahedin, there is no process of ordering the El Mujahedin to hand over, is there? Would you agree that this is unusual?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry once again, but I'm still having trouble understanding. You can't go from a relationship between two organs, on the one hand, a unit, and, on the other hand, the Military Police Battalion, you can't move from that to a relationship between other entities, the unit, on the one hand, and the Military Security Service, because the last two organs are different from the first two. So please, Mr. Robson, so that the Chamber can understand and so as to avoid any confusion, could you please ask questions while talking about the same kind of relationship at the same level, please. To clarify what I've just said: Here, we're not talking about the Military Security Service; we are talking about the Military Police Battalion. So please remain focused on the same organs and on the same relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just picking up from where the witness last gave us his answer.
