He stated that the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps could issue an order through the professional lines to the security organ within a subordinate detachment, at least that's how I understood his testimony. What I am asking him is that: If the El Mujahedin Detachment had been correctly within the system of reporting, let's call it, below the 3rd Corps, then similarly the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps could have issued an order directly to the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment. That's what I'm trying to clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree with you. If you allow, Mr. Robson, I will turn directly to the witness and ask him a question. Mr. Robson presented an assumption to you, and he talked about the relationship between one unit and the Military Security Service; and on the basis of your testimony, I think it appears clearly that the military security organ of the unit, including the detachment, is subordinated to the military security organ at the highest level. That I understood. However, I still have a problem, because here in that document, we are talking about another relationship, a relationship between a unit, to be more specific the El Mujahedin Detachment, and the Military Police Battalion. Therefore, as regards the assumption presented to you by Mr. Robson as regards a different unit, i.e., not the El Mujahedin Detachment but another unit belonging to your army, I would like to know if the security organ of the unit could receive an order from the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, if I can ask you again, this document speaks of a security body of the El Mujahedin Detachment. You have told us that the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps had the ability to issue orders directly to subordinate units through the professional line. My question is: If the El Mujahedin Detachment had been functioning as a regular unit of the ARBiH, could the Military Security Service organ have issued an order to the security body of the El Mujahedin Detachment and simply ordered them to hand over these Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The security organ of the 3rd Corps could, through the command-and-control system, issue an order to the security organ of the detachment to hand over the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in such a situation, there would not be any need for any agreement to take place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An agreement within the command-and-control system of an army? Well, there shouldn't be one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just before we leave this document, I have a quick question for you. The document talks about the hand-over of members of the VRS and that the hand-over took place on the 29th of September, 1995. Can you explain for us why the document bears the date the 19th of October, 1995? Would I be right in saying that you would expect the hand over document to be signed contemporaneously at the time and date that the hand-over actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An integral element of the hand-over should be a list of the persons handed over, which should be kept by both sides. I cannot comment on the difference between the dates, since I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would it be usual for a hand-over document to be prepared on the day that the hand-over actually takes place?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we could have expected that the date at the top of this document would have been the 29th of September, 1995; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of any situations where members of the military police subsequently returned back to a place or unit where a hand-over occurred for -- to sign a retrospective hand-over document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll move on to a new issue and try and deal with this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that during the war in Central Bosnia, there were a lot of men from countries outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as from North African countries, Turkey, the Middle East, and other places?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And was it common for these men to be collectively referred to as "Arabs"?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a common term used by various people because they more or less looked alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Some of these men from foreign countries would work in Central Bosnia for humanitarian organisations and other organisations as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Central Bosnia, there were several organisations within which a number of foreign citizens worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that apart from the El Mujahedin Detachment, there were other Mujahedin groups that existed in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you recall where any of those other Mujahedin groups were based?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any specific details since I wasn't there, but I heard of some parts of Travnik, towards the area of the 7th Corps, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it right that sometimes, if a person gave a report to the civilian police that a crime had been committed by an Arab, the civilian police would often simply say that the crime had been committed by a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment, without carrying out any further checks?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll have to object to that. Mr. Robson is asking this -- a question of this witness for which he has no professed competency to answer. He's asking about the civilian police, if the civilian police discovered something, they would have reported it a specific way. This witness is a military police officer. I don't believe that he would have direct knowledge about this, and I believe that any answer he would give in that regard would be irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can clarify that with the witness. I certainly would not ask him to speculate. I'm only asking him to answer based on his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I do think you are asking a speculative question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As a member of the -- as the commander of the 3rd Military Police Battalion, did you have any dealings with the civilian police in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you ever receive information from the civilian police about Mujahedin members?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw a note somewhere in which a theft was reported. The civilian police forwarded it to us for further processing, since the perpetrators were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Often, such information was not verified, since the easiest thing was to merely state that someone was a member of this and that military formation so as to avoid their further authority in the matter, without corroborating anything by any documents which would serve to prove that the given person was a member of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And focusing on the members of the Military Police Battalion, again, would military police officers, if they received information that a crime had been committed by an Arab or a foreigner, would they often simply say it was committed by a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment, without carrying out any further inquiries?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Military Police Battalion, first and foremost, on the spot had to establish the circumstances under which the crime had been committed. They were also supposed to conduct eyewitness interviews and to try and determine the identity of the perpetrators by trying to gain certain information on how those people looked, behaved, and similar; and then to follow up that investigation by trying, if possible, to establish whether that person or persons were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, or any other unit for that matter. In the final stage, provided all this has been established, if that person was indeed a member of the army, then legal steps are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And sometimes was it -- let me show you a document that the Prosecution used yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's P1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 870.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, this document, when it appears, it's an official record dated the 19th of March, 1995, from the Military Police 3rd Battalion, and it refers to a person by the name of Dragutin Botic. Can you remember this document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What we can see from this document is that the 3rd Military Police Battalion was summoned to the premises of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and that was in response to a request for assistance from the detachment itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see that the man mentioned, Dragutin Botic, had been created problems for the detachment and that the Military Police Battalion took him away. Now, if we look at paragraph 2, can you confirm that when the Military Police Battalion took Mr. Botic away, they recorded the physical condition that they found him in, didn't they? We can see that they recorded the injuries that he had to his face?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So does it follow from this that in such a situation, when persons were handed over to the military police, it was common practice for the military police to record the physical state of the person that they took over; and if they saw injuries on the person, they would record that on a note?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document can be put away. If we can briefly turn to P2705. While we're waiting for the document, I can explain that this is a daily report of the 3rd Police Battalion, dated the 7th of October, 1995, and it's sent to the -- it was sent to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps. If we can just turn to the last page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, we've seen a number of these reports now. Can you confirm that that is your name and signature at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my name, but the signature is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Has somebody signed the document for you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The person who was authorised to sign on behalf of the commander, Dzemal Muharemovic, he was the commander of the logistics company.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, in this document, is page number 5 in the English version, and in the B/C/S I believe it might be page number 3. It's page number 2. I apologise. If it can be brought down in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you see there a heading which states -- well, perhaps you can read out for us what the heading says exactly.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Engagement of desk officers of the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, paragraph C, can you confirm that what this talks about is that the Zenica military prosecutor received documents in connection with criminal proceedings of the 23rd of September, 1995, which the 3rd Military Police Battalion instituted against Sefik Bijelo, a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear from this portion of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So from this document, can we conclude that in October 1995, the 3rd Military Police Battalion did submit at least one criminal report against members of the El Mujahedin Detachment to a competent military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this document could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 880.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could refer now to Exhibit 872. While we're waiting for the document to appear, if I could explain that the document we're about to see is a report from the 3rd Military Police Battalion to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps, dated the 7th of September, 1995. If we can just scroll to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version, and if we can go to the second page, please, to ascertain the author.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, we can see that it bears your name. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you know who signed the document for you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Logistics Company, Dzemal Muharemovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can return to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: This report refers to members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. It refers to criminal acts that they are purported to have carried out. Are you able to explain, if there was information that criminal offences had been carried out by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and information about their identities were known, were steps taken to investigate further and arrest these members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the document I have before me, I can tell you that this is an -- this is information rather than a report. It involves things and acts committed within the area of responsibility of the 7th Corps. The purpose of forwarding the information was to coordinate the activities with the security sector of the 3rd Corps. That means that the MP Battalion did not have territorial jurisdiction or competence for this particular situation; therefore, they asked that the military security sector of the 3rd Corps, via the security service of the 7th Corps, that they intervene in order to establish who the perpetrators of the acts mentioned here are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So from this document, we are unable to tell whether or not further steps were taken to investigate and arrest the persons mentioned within this report?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this document, I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we can put this document away, and if I can turn to events in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that at no point on the 11th of September, 1995, or any other date, did you receive a call from or information from the 328th Brigade that your military police unit should come and collect prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no information, order, or call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you also confirm that you did not receive information from any source that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment had been involved in serious crimes during the Ozren-Vozuca action in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive a single piece of information of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, according to what you told the Office of the Prosecution when you were interviewed on the 6th of November of 2007, very recently - and this is at paragraph 65 - you stated: "I must say that I did not have any information about prisoners of war being mistreated in the camp of the El Mujahedin Detachment." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember having said that, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we've seen, from at least one document and today just a moment ago, that criminal charges have or had been filed against members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Can we conclude that if you had received information that members of the El Mujahedin Detachment had been involved in serious criminal acts, you would have taken steps to investigate the matter and file a criminal report against them?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I received such information, first of all, I'd inform the chief of security of the 3rd Corps, and I believe we would coordinate our activities from that point onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, I want to ask you about Maline and Bikosi, because yesterday the Prosecutor asked you if an investigation was carried out into events in the village of Maline/Bikosi. My question is: If an investigation had been carried out by a unit subordinate to you into events occurring at those locations, you would not necessarily know about such an investigation, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was my direct subordinate, that unit, that is, I would have to know about it, not in other cases [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm told that the transcript didn't capture your answer correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did you say: If it was not a direct subordinate, you would not have to know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. If it is a directly subordinated unit, I have to know about it; if it's not, then, of course, I don't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if an investigation into events in Maline/Bikosi had been carried out by the Military Security Service, rather than the military police, again you didn't have to know about such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions. Thank you for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 867 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, a question was put to you about the distribution list that we see at the bottom of the first page there, directly adjacent to your signature. Do you see "the 328th Brigade" on this distribution list?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see "the 329th Brigade" on this distribution list?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you know why those units wouldn't have received this document as well?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. My signature was placed here to confirm the authenticity rather than to authorise the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I would like to bring another document up, Your Honour. Given the time, it might be appropriate to just do this after the break. I see it's around noon already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: On reflection, Your Honour, I've come to the conclusion that the Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, I would simply like to ask you if you could confirm whether I have understood correctly, whether the El Mujahedin Detachment did not have a security organ, a military security organ, or did the El Mujahedin Detachment have such an organ?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state with certainty that it did have an organ; but according to establishment, it should definitely have had a security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did the El Mujahedin Detachment have a military police service?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. And now I would like to have a better understanding with regard to the chain of command and control with regard to possible violations, because here we are dealing with simple allegations, and I emphasise, allegations of violations of these various rules, rules that we looked at this morning that seemed quite complete, and, well, especially during a period of war there is a significant risk that such rules not be complied with. If a subordinate unit did not fulfill its duties, its obligations to investigate, for example, to verify and to control its soldiers, namely, the command of the unit with regard to his subordinates, again within the unit, whose duty was it to take steps should this happen?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs were the first that needed to point out the fact that certain -- a certain unit was not sanctioning violations or certain acts; and on that basis, the security service would need to compile all the information, and, then, along the line of command, insist that the commands take measures in terms of punishing the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I've understood you correctly, if I followed correctly the examination and cross-examination, this went up to the command -- the commander of the 3rd Corps, this line of command and control. We looked at some of the orders, and now I'm interested in some of the possible omissions. With regard to such omissions, could we go all the way up to the line of command and control, in fact higher up than the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that, because the level that I was at practically ended with the 3rd Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I have one last point of clarification. Witness, you, yourself personally, did you have a duty to investigate whenever a crime was notified to you, when you were informed of a crime that had been committed, to investigate simply on the basis of rumours; in other words, notice of this crime or information about this crime did not come from an official source?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the eventuality that certain information was acquired about a committed violation, it was my duty to make an Official Note and inform the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what I'm interested in is knowing whether, in order for you to begin an inquiry or an investigation, did the information have to come from an official source or was it enough for the information to come from any source, whatever source, even if it was not official, even if there were only rumours, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively from an official source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Now, sir, can I just find out from you, what kind of misdemeanor or -- let me back off. How would you categorize a failure or refusal to hand over prisoners of war by a unit? Would you categorize that as something that calls for disciplinary action or would you categorize that as a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was a strict refusal of an order, then in any case it would be categorized as a criminal offence. If a unit refused and there was an order that it had to carry out, then it would be a criminal offence categorized as a refusal to carry out an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if it was reported to you, that is, your unit, that a particular unit is refusing to do so, what steps will you take?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle is the same again; meaning, inform the chief of the 3rd Corps Military Security Service, ask him for further instructions, in terms of taking measures, because the military police, or specifically the MP Battalion, did not have the authority to enter the composition of a different unit and carry out, thereby, any investigations or other actions, without having an order for that from the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I saw this morning, on your rules and duties and tasks, that both the Military Police Battalion and the security services organ had the right, if a member of the army commits a crime, to arrest him, and you did tell us that you didn't need anybody else's permission to do so, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the rule states that if at the point of time when the act was committed, or according to absolute information that the person did carry out said criminal offence, we established that the military police is authorised to carry out the arrest or to submit a report. So the military police would find a person at a certain location carrying out a criminal act, then they would have the authority to arrest him, hand him over to the prosecutor whose jurisdiction that was, and they would also have the right to submit a report or file a report. But to enter a unit and then carry out an investigation without the chief of the security service having issued an order for that first, or approved the security organ of that unit to allow the entry to the members of the military police, without that, without those steps, this would not be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, sir, I am finding your answer very difficult to understand. I'm putting to you a situation where a unit refuses. Now, you're telling me that you need to get an order from a superior, ordering the person who's refusing to allow you. He's refusing. He's being obstinate. You have to make sure that law and order is observed.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Law must be observed, but refusal of an order has to be based on law or an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, this person just says, "I refuse."

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he didn't refuse that to me. I don't know. I never had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, sir, what do you do? You get that report. What would you do? Surely, from the answer you've given, I can see two possibilities. Well, I see two possibilities coming from the answer you gave and the way I understood your tasks and duties this morning. The way I understood your tasks and duties this morning, you don't need anybody's order, you can go and investigate, and arrest. But you are saying, in your answer, you would need an order from a superior. I would expect you to say, "If I got that notice, I would approach my superior for an order to enable me to go and do the search," wouldn't you. Wouldn't you do that? Wasn't that what you ought to do?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're saying you can't do that without an order coming up, you know, as if the order must just come. But isn't it incumbent upon you to go and ask for that order, if indeed you must get it?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have the information, yes, then it's up to me to request such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if subordinate units then don't report to you, because according to what you told us, you never received any report of the El Mujahedin Detachment breaking the law, did I hear you correctly in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And now we have heard evidence that there are some times when they have refused to hand over POWs and handed them over much later, and the surprising thing is that you say you never received this report.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the chain of command, we didn't have the option of receiving information like that. The Military Security Service, along its own line, practically had that information, in terms of capture, detention, and all the other activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And based on the rules and regulations that we saw this morning that govern them, would they also then have the duty to go and investigate under those circumstances and arrest the person who was refusing to hand over?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have that duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if a subordinate unit did not carry out that, let's say they go and ask for POWs and the POWs are not handed over and they say, "There's nothing we can do," and they leave it there, how would you categorize that behaviour by that subordinate unit that doesn't carry the matter any further?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As disobedience, non-observance of orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As I understand your evidence, Mr. Mujezinovic - and this is in respect of a question by Judge Lattanzi - in theory, according to establishment, the El Mujahedin should have had a security organ; however, is it the case that, in fact, you don't know whether or not that detachment had such a security organ?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM MUJEZINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I personally never had any contacts with anyone from the El Mujahedin Detachment, so I really cannot say if there was a security organ there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, sir. That brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you so much for coming to testify. I hope you have a pleasant trip back home. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Travel well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution next calls Mr. Muris Hadziselimovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hadziselimovic. Could you please tell the Court your profession?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I am Muris Hadziselimovic. At the moment, I'm the chief prosecutor in the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office of the Zenica-Doboj Canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can the Trial Chamber assume from that, then, sir, that you're trained as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber the training you received, the legal training?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I completed law school in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what year was that, sir, if you don't mind saying?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In December 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You told the Trial Chamber you're currently the chief prosecutor at the Zenica-Doboj Cantonal Prosecutor's Office. What job did you have in 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, March 1st, I assumed the duty of deputy prosecutor in the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office; and that entire year, I carried out those duties until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what job did you hold starting in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: First, I was deputy of the Higher Public Prosecution Office in Zenica; and then from mid 1997, I was deputy municipal public prosecutor in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And after that, sir, starting in 1997?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: From 2001, I was the municipal public prosecutor in Zenica, until the 22nd of March, 2004, when I was appointed to the duties that I am currently carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, could you explain to the Court, what are your duties as the chief prosecutor of the Zenica-Doboj Cantonal Prosecutor's Office now?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure, I was the person authorised to find out and prosecute perpetrators of criminal acts. Together with me, I had two deputies in the prosecutor's office and 22 cantonal prosecutors. All of them had the option of representing me before courts and in investigations before the prosecutor's office. I was the chief of the prosecutor's office; and in that role, I contacted all the organs, state and other organs, and I can also appear in proceedings before courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, I see that the way it's been translated, at least, you're speaking in the past tense, that you were the person authorised and so on. Just to clarify, you still hold this position, chief prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we've had some names of various courts appear in the transcript here, and I wonder if you might explain to the Trial Chamber what the Higher Public Prosecution Office is, where you were in 1997, and the Zenica-Doboj Cantonal Prosecutor's Office, where you are now; that is to say, what is the relationship between those two courts [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Courts or the prosecutor's offices? It's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Courts -- I'm sorry, prosecutor's offices, yes.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The actual jurisdictions are practically the same. The Cantonal Prosecutor's Office, within the current organisational system, has a broader authority, while the district jurisdiction is almost the same. I will try to explain that. The Higher Public Prosecution Office in Zenica had local jurisdiction for several municipalities, and the municipalities more or less were Zenica, Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj, and a part of Tesanj; and then Kakanj, Visoko, Breza, Travnik, a part of the Vitez Municipality, Bugojno, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce. The actual jurisdiction was for graver criminal acts, such as war crimes and homicides, or grave criminal acts committed in relation to property. The Cantonal Prosecutor's Office, according to the current structure, organisation, and the law, has local jurisdiction over all of these mentioned municipalities, just like the Higher Public Prosecution Office, except for Travnik, Bugojno, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce. As I said, the actual jurisdiction was much broader, because we are the only ones who can prosecute perpetrators for all kinds of the criminal acts that are laid down in the Criminal Code of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is there such a thing now as the Higher Public Prosecution Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did that institute exist in 1993 and in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were in the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office in 1993. What was the territorial jurisdiction of the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office and of the Zenica District Military Court in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It more or less coincided with the jurisdiction of the Higher Public Prosecution Office or the Higher Court in Zenica, but I don't know exactly. I'm not sure when the District Military Prosecutor's Office was formed with its seat in Travnik, because from that point on those types of cases were taken over by that prosecutor's office and the court in Travnik. The rest, of course, the ones in the free territory, there was the local or the territorial jurisdiction of the District Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So speaking of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. When you say "from that point," are you referring to time; and if so, when? What is the time? You said: "From that point on, those types of cases were taken over by the prosecutor's office." Which point is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does have to do with the point in time, but I cannot tell you precisely as of what date it is. I don't know whether it was in 1993 or 1994. That is why I cannot tell you what the year was. However, I know that from that point on, cases were taken over by the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Speaking specifically of Zavidovici Municipality, in whose territorial jurisdiction did Zavidovici Municipality fall in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As regards local jurisdiction over Zavidovici Municipality, it was possible that both the Municipal Public Prosecutor's office as well as the Higher Public Prosecution Office be competent, as well as the Higher Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Speaking exclusively of the District Military Prosecutor's Office in 1993 and 1995, was Zavidovici Municipality within the territorial jurisdiction of the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have the witness shown, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before he gets shown something, you sort of alluded to the fact that at least three courts, the Municipal Public Prosecutor's Office, as well as the Higher Public Prosecution Office and the Higher Military Prosecutor's office, had concurrent jurisdiction. Are you talking of concurrent jurisdiction in terms of crimes or in terms of area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Territorially speaking, all of them were competent. Their jurisdictions differed, though. That is why it couldn't happen that they interfere with each other's jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the difference in jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, the division of jurisdictions between the Higher Public Prosecution Office and the District Military Prosecutor's Office was in the fact -- or rather, in who perpetrated a crime. If it is a serviceman, then it was under the competence of the Military Prosecutor's Office who would institute proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean by "servicemen"? Service in what? Sorry. This is how the interpreter said it: "If it is a serviceman, then it was under the competence of the Military Prosecutor's Office..." Service in the municipality, service in the state, service in what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Servicemen as soldiers with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then you're saying, if it was a serviceman in the army, it would fall under the Military Prosecutor's Office, right, and then the others? Civilians would fall under the other courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, depending on the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If Your Honour is satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If Exhibit 25 could be shown to the witness, I believe this might help to illuminate this issue as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention in particular to Article 6, which is on page 2 of both. If you could take a look at Article 6, please, Mr. Hadziselimovic, does that describe the subject matter jurisdiction of the District Military Prosecutor's Office -- I'm sorry, of the courts, that is?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We have here the subject matter jurisdiction of the courts, and it tallied with the subject matter jurisdiction for all of the prosecutor's offices that were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Other than the District Military Prosecutor's Office, was there any other institution or organisation that had the competency to prosecute crimes committed by military service members in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: District Military Prosecutor's Offices and the courts were the only ones competent to establish the identity and prosecute perpetrators of crimes, provided the perpetrators are soldiers, army members. There was one exception, though, regulated by the law as well as by the jurisprudence. If a person is a member of the army, and if there is a civilian involved as an accomplice, in that case the Higher Military Prosecutors Office and the Higher Court were competent. That was the only exemption from the general rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which higher court, high military court or just a High Civilian Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no higher military court. The Higher Court or the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Speaking more specifically about your time as a district military prosecutor, could you please tell the Trial Chamber your primary duties as district military prosecutor from 1993 until 1996?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The basic duty was to prosecute criminal offenders. In that regard, we applied all possible procedural-legal issues. We could, for example, initiate an investigation by applying for it to be opened. It would be conducted by an investigative judge of the District Military Court. After that, or rather, once the investigation is completed, we wouldn't have to make the so-called "prosecutor's decision." We could abandon further investigation, or we could also choose to have an indictment issued. Should that happen, the main hearing would be scheduled immediately, and it was our duty to present the indictment during the main hearing. Once a judgement would be handed down by the Bench, we could appeal their decision, and it was also one of our duties, or obligations rather, or one of our competences, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Who was your superior or what was the title of your superior when you were in the District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was deputy district military prosecutor. My superior was the district military prosecutor. That was his title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: How many other deputies were in the office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the existence of the District Military Prosecutor's Office, there were four deputies; however, some people left, some people came on board. Perhaps at a given point, there may have been only three, and then four again. But, in any case, there were three to four deputy prosecutors at any given time working on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You said, sir, on page 75, at lines 23 and 24, that you could, "for example, initiate an investigation by applying for it to be opened." Was there any other way that investigations were opened or conducted, independent of whether or not you asked for them to be opened?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: According to the then law on criminal procedure, there was no other way. The exclusive jurisdiction of the investigative judge was to conduct investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was the involvement of the military police or any police authorities in this process?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Their role in a criminal proceedings was the so-called "pre-trial" or rather, "pre-investigative" part of the proceedings. They would have to conduct all investigative procedures. They would have to complete a file, and send it to the competent district prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And when that file came in to the district prosecutor's office, how in any way was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Anything that would come in to the district prosecutor's office, all correspondence that was delivered was registered. We had a registry. Then the district military prosecutor would go through the mail and the reports, and he would do the so-called "allocation." He would decide on which type of books each of the items would be registered; and then, again, that would be done by the registry office. If there was a criminal report in question, they would put it in a particular logbook, thus registering that report, and that would be the end of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned that they would put it in a particular logbook. How many logbooks did the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Zenica maintain?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: There was only one logbook, but I don't know how many logbooks have been used up during the time the district military -- the district prosecutor's office was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a clarification on the previous answer you gave, sir. You said, "If there was a criminal report in question, they would put it in a particular logbook, thus registering that report, and that would be the end of the procedure." Would it not be for you, then, to investigate and determine whether to prosecute, or to go to the investigative judge to investigate whether there is a case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps you have misunderstood me. I was merely talking about registering documents. The procedure would then be that the district prosecutor would task a particular deputy with a given number of cases, which then they would process further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just needed that to be clarified. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What sort of data --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I was just waiting for the interpretation to be complete. I'd like to remind you that there is a slight lag between the English and the French. I would like to put a question to the witness. Sir, did you have an obligation to prosecute or was it only an option that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a clarification? Does it pertain to me, personally, as deputy, or to something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the office as a whole, your office, and I'm talking about the prosecutor's office, the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as each individual case goes, each of the deputies that was tasked with a certain case had a freedom to choose whether to prosecute further or whether he should state that either there was no criminal offence or that it was not committed by that particular person, and then the proceedings would cease. Occasionally, consultation was needed with the district prosecutor, since he was the person responsible for the overall jurisdiction. It could happen that once we would notify the district prosecutor, he would be dissatisfied with our decision, and then there would be a discussion, during which he could say that his decision was final; and if it was contrary to ours, he could order us to do what he wanted us to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I wanted to ask you something else. If a suspect was still a suspect, if there were still suspicions, would the District Military Prosecutor's Office be obliged to prosecute a suspect or did it only have the ability to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say I fail to understand your question fully. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of suspicions, and when you continued to have suspicions, were you obliged to initiate proceedings, or could you simply decide to not pursue the proceedings, to bring them to an end? Did you have that option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We acted in accordance with the law. If there was a criminal offence committed, we would initiate a proceedings. If I understood correctly, well, I'll try to answer. If there is a suspect against whom proceedings are instituted, and if that person is still free and continues to commit crimes, I believe you asked me whether we would be under an obligation to prosecute him. I have to tell you that during that period, the prosecutor's office did not have the technical or legal means to deal with the issue of detecting crimes. We would merely follow up on criminal reports or reports of the military police, and even the civilian police could submit their own report to us. It means this: It was our duty to follow it up if there was a criminal report or a report on a crime committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That does clear things up, the last part, the last sentence of your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the criminal reports that are filed and the logbook, could you please tell the Chamber what sort of data would be recorded in the logbook when a criminal report would come in; that is, come into the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to delineate. The entry logbook would be the one registering everything, all correspondence that would come to our office. What was important was who sent it and when it was received. Based on the prosecutor's decision and based on his allocation, it would then be registered in a different logbook called "KT logbook," including all information that would be found in the given criminal report. If that is what you meant, I can tell you that each criminal report would receive a number, a file number; also, first and last names of suspects would be included; then the relevant legal law -- the relevant article of the law and the crimes that the suspects are suspected of having committed; then also the name of the victim, if there was any; the time and place of the act. Those were the columns important for the first round of registration. That would include the data from the criminal reports. All other data that would be registered would have to do with any activities on the part of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned there was an entry logbook and there was a KT logbook. Were there any other logbooks in use at the time?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The KT logbook would include criminal reports submitted against adult perpetrators and identified adult perpetrators; then there was a KTN logbook which would only refer to perpetrators which had not been identified at the moment the criminal report was submitted; then there was the KTA logbook, and this would include reports on an event, but the perpetrator of which was unknown. At the outset, we wouldn't know whether the act committed is indeed an offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, then, were all criminal reports, received from any agency, logged or recorded in one of these three logbooks: KT, KTN, or KTA?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can also tell you that there was a KTM logbook for minors; however, there were very few. Minors were not military conscripts; however, we had such a logbook as well. The criminal report would have to be recorded in either of the books, in one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What about when results of an investigation came back from an investigative judge, would those also be recorded in one of these logbooks?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. It was the KT logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if you could tell the Trial Chamber, please, why was it important that this, these criminal reports and this particular data, be recorded in this particular way?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was our legal obligation to have all criminal reports registered into the books, and it was also regulated by our internal regulation. Everything received by the prosecutor's office had to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, what criminal codes were in effect in 1993 and 1995; that is, what criminal codes were you prosecuting under in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Criminal Law taken over from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could bring up Exhibit number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And looking at the first page of it, can you determine what precisely this document is?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the Criminal Law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, taken in 1992 by the Presidency, and it was applied as the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did this Criminal Code include, for example, any war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did this Criminal Code include any offences involving deaths or, for example, murder?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we can go to page 36 -- I'm sorry, page 22 of the English, page 18 of the B/C/S, and in particular Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is this the statute under which you would prosecute a murder?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this can be put away now, Your Honour. If we could see Exhibit 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recognise what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which, I repeat, under a decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was taken as the law in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Were there any statutes in this Criminal Code involving war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you recall generally what articles war crimes would cover within this statute, this Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: These articles from 141 to 149 or 150. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So just to clarify, sir, these two criminal codes that I showed you, they were both in effect concurrently in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And these criminal codes would also have applied to military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Witness. Did you not have a military criminal code?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could, in this document, go to page 69 in the English, page 66 in the Bosnian. Scroll down to Article 142 in the English, or perhaps go to the next page if that's necessary. I see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we can see in Article 142 that this says: "War crimes against the civilian population." Can you tell the Trial Chamber generally, sir, what was the difference between a war crime that would have been charged under Articles 142 to 149 of this Code and a murder that would have been charged under the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The key thing or the way to differentiate is that for an act that constituted a war crime, you could charge someone who committed that in a specific time period, and for Bosnia and Herzegovina that was from the 1st of January, 1991, until the signing of the Dayton Accords on the 22nd and the 23rd of December, 1995. So somebody could be suspected of having committed a war crime for that in any form in that period. Secondly, an important fact was that these acts could mainly have been perpetrated by military personnel, members of the army, of course also by members of some other formations. Although in the articles itself, this is not stated because maybe you can see who, in committing the rules or violating the rules, so it's not specified. It doesn't say military personnel committing these acts. The practice was that such criminal acts could have been perpetrated only by members of military formations, in the broadest sense of the word. Of course, there were those who, as civilian officials, could also have perpetrated such criminal acts. The third important thing was that the citizens of those who had been injured parties, who were either citizens or members of the injured party. So these are the three categories under which it would be determined if a specific act would be treated as a murder, or a war crime, or a murder as part of the commission of a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What, specifically, was important about the status of the victims or the injured party in the determination of whether a crime was a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, the fact that they were in a subordinate position in the territory that was under the control of any military formation or authority, civilian authority, if we're talking about the population of different ethnicities or that was of a different ethnicity from those actually executing the authority, and most frequently that was the case. For example, the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, what the significant thing here would be that there were Bosnians or Croats there who could be the subjects of the perpetration of a war crime. So we would have different ethnic groups involved here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is ethnicity the only determining factor about whether something would be a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the only determining factor, but it was a crucial factor. In the broadest sense, this was the civilian population which was protected under the Geneva Conventions, which were being applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So any acts or treatment in relation to them, if it contravened the Geneva Conventions, would imply that this would be under or covered by this article of the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You mentioned civilian population and the Geneva Convention. Did that also apply to prisoners of war, for example?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I think that there was a decision by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where it was stated that all the Geneva Conventions were to be applied in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including those that referred to prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm at a position now where I was about to explore this a little bit further by showing an additional document. I see that it's 1343. I don't know if this is an appropriate time for the Court to break. But I'm just thinking, the amount of time it takes to load the document itself, we might not have time for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we haven't finished with you, sir. You'll have to come back on Tuesday, the 27th of November, at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. Unfortunately, we are not going to be sitting on Monday, so you'll have to come on Tuesday. Court adjourned until to Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
